front: What is a Kubernetes controller?
back: A control loop running in the kube-controller-manager that watches the cluster's current state via the API server and makes changes to drive it toward the declared desired state (e.g. keeping a set number of pods running).
source: Managing Kubernetes Controllers and Deployments — Introduction to Controllers

front: What is a DaemonSet and when do you use one?
back: A controller that ensures one copy of a pod runs on every node (or a subset). Adding a node automatically schedules a pod there. Used for per-node background tasks like log collection, monitoring, and kube-proxy.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Choosing the Right Workload Controller

front: How does a StatefulSet differ from a Deployment?
back: A StatefulSet is for stateful apps (databases) and gives each pod a stable, unique identity (e.g. db-0) with persistent storage and ordered scaling/updates. A Deployment is for stateless apps where every pod is interchangeable.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Choosing the Right Workload Controller

front: What is the difference between a Job and a CronJob?
back: A Job creates pods and ensures a defined number terminate successfully, then stops. A CronJob creates and manages Jobs on a recurring schedule (cron syntax), e.g. a nightly backup.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Choosing the Right Workload Controller

front: What do the Job fields completions and parallelism control?
back: completions = number of required successful pod runs before the Job is complete. parallelism = maximum number of pods allowed to run at the same time. completions:6, parallelism:2 runs six successes in batches of two.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Demo: Managing Batch Workloads

front: What are the three required elements of a ReplicaSet (and Deployment) spec?
back: replicas (desired pod count), a selector (matchLabels or matchExpressions, determining membership), and a pod template (the pod definition to create).
source: Managing Kubernetes Controllers and Deployments — Understanding ReplicaSet Controller Operations

front: What is an orphan pod?
back: A pod whose label was changed so it no longer matches its controller's selector (or whose controller was deleted with --cascade=orphan). The controller no longer manages it, so it is not deleted when the controller is, and a new pod is created to replace it in the set.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Demo: Managing Long-running Workloads

front: How do you imperatively create a deployment and scale it to 5 replicas?
back: kubectl create deployment hello-world --image= ; then kubectl scale deployment hello-world --replicas=5
source: Managing Kubernetes Controllers and Deployments — Demo: Creating a Basic Deployment

front: What change triggers a Deployment rollout?
back: Only a change to the pod template (container image, env vars, labels, restart policy, etc.). Changing other deployment-spec fields like replicas does NOT trigger a rollout — it just scales.
source: Managing Kubernetes Controllers and Deployments — Updating a Deployment and Checking Rollout Status

front: What do maxSurge and maxUnavailable do in a RollingUpdate?
back: maxSurge = max extra pods allowed above the desired count during the update (default 25%). maxUnavailable = max pods that can be unavailable during the update (default 25%). Both accept a percentage or integer.
source: Managing Kubernetes Controllers and Deployments — Controlling Updates with UpdateStrategy

front: When would you use the Recreate update strategy instead of RollingUpdate?
back: When the new and old versions cannot run concurrently (e.g. data-structure or persistent-state conflicts). Recreate terminates all old pods first, then starts the new ones — guaranteed downtime, but never two versions at once.
source: Managing Kubernetes Controllers and Deployments — Controlling Updates with UpdateStrategy

front: How do you view rollout history and roll back to revision 2?
back: kubectl rollout history deployment hello-world ; (inspect with --revision=2) ; kubectl rollout undo deployment hello-world --to-revision=2
source: Managing Kubernetes Controllers and Deployments — Pausing and Rolling Back Deployments

front: How many deployment revisions does Kubernetes keep, and how do you change it?
back: By default 10 revisions (old ReplicaSets). Set the revisionHistoryLimit field in the deployment spec to change it; 0 cleans up old ReplicaSets immediately.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Rollback and Revision History

front: What are the two ways to inject a ConfigMap or Secret into a pod, and which supports hot reload?
back: As environment variables (envFrom / valueFrom) — no hot reload, must restart the pod. Or as volume mounts — supports hot reload when you mount a whole directory (not a single file).
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Decoupling Configuration

front: How do you create a Secret from a literal and inject it as env vars?
back: kubectl create secret generic db-pass --from-literal=DB_PWD='K8sRocks!' ; then in the container add envFrom: - secretRef: { name: db-pass }
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Demo: Mounting Secrets into a Pod

front: Are Kubernetes Secrets encrypted by default?
back: No. Secret values are only Base64-encoded (obscured, not secured) and stored in etcd. Harden with etcd encryption at rest, RBAC least privilege on get/watch/list, mounting only into the container that needs it, and external providers like Vault.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Managing Secrets

front: What is the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)?
back: A built-in controller (in kube-controller-manager) that scales the number of replicas of a Deployment or StatefulSet based on metrics like CPU/memory from the metrics server, comparing actual usage to a target.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Autoscaling Workloads

front: How do you create an HPA targeting 50% CPU, min 1, max 10 replicas?
back: kubectl autoscale deployment hello-world --cpu-percent=50 --min=1 --max=10. The target pods must have resource requests defined and the metrics server running.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Demo: Configuring HPA

front: What is the difference between a livenessProbe and a readinessProbe on failure?
back: livenessProbe failure → the kubelet restarts the container (per restart policy). readinessProbe failure → the pod's IP is removed from Service endpoints (no restart), so it stops receiving traffic.
source: Managing the Kubernetes API Server and Pods — Defining Pod Health

front: What is a startupProbe used for?
back: For apps with long startup times. While the startupProbe runs, liveness and readiness probes are disabled; once it succeeds they take over. On startupProbe failure the kubelet restarts the container per the restart policy.
source: Managing the Kubernetes API Server and Pods — Defining Pod Health

front: What are the three probe diagnostic check types?
back: exec (run a command; exit code 0 = success), tcpSocket (open a TCP port successfully), and httpGet (HTTP response code >=200 and <400 = success).
source: Managing the Kubernetes API Server and Pods — Defining Pod Health

front: How do resource requests and limits differ, and what happens when limits are exceeded?
back: requests = guaranteed resources used by the scheduler to place the pod. limits = hard ceiling. Exceeding the CPU limit throttles the container; exceeding the memory limit gets it OOMKilled by the kernel.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Configuring Pod Admission

front: What are the three QoS classes and how are they assigned?
back: Guaranteed (requests == limits for both CPU and memory; highest priority), Burstable (requests < limits), BestEffort (no requests/limits; lowest, evicted first under memory pressure).
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Configuring Pod Admission

front: What are the three taint effects?
back: NoSchedule (no new untolerated pod is scheduled), PreferNoSchedule (scheduler tries to avoid the node), and NoExecute (existing untolerated pods are evicted). A pod needs a matching toleration to be placed on a tainted node.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Demo: Taints and Tolerations

front: How do you create a static pod and why can't you delete it with kubectl?
back: Place a pod manifest in the node's staticPodPath (default /etc/kubernetes/manifests). The kubelet manages it, not the API server, and exposes a read-only mirror pod. kubectl delete won't remove it — delete the manifest file from the path instead.
source: Managing the Kubernetes API Server and Pods — Introducing and Working Static Pods

front: What does a Pod Disruption Budget (PDB) protect against?
back: Voluntary disruptions (node drains, upgrades, scaling down pools) — not involuntary failures. Using minAvailable or maxUnavailable, it blocks evictions (e.g. kubectl drain) that would breach the floor until a replacement pod is running.
source: Workloads and Scheduling for CKA — Pod Disruption Budgets

front: How do you generate boilerplate YAML for any resource quickly?
back: Combine an imperative command with --dry-run=client -o yaml, e.g. kubectl create deployment nginx --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml. Many use an alias like export do='--dry-run=client -o yaml'.
source: Managing the Kubernetes API Server and Pods — Using kubectl dry-run
